content_metadata.description: A comprehensive video introducing the concepts and activities involved in a physics lab focused on one-dimensional motion. activities.description: Professor introduces the concept of one-dimensional motion.
Professor explains the first part of the lab, measuring one-dimensional motion by walking back and forth in front of a sonic motion detector.
Professor explains how the sonic motion detector works using chirps of sound.
Professor discusses predetermined graphs in Logger Pro and the goal of matching those graphs with body movement.
Professor explains the possibility of aliasing effects and their cause.
Professor encourages students to think about how to be a better echo material for the sensor.
Professor explains the second part of the lab, throwing a tennis ball up and down while filming with a camera.
Professor explains analyzing the ball's motion in Logger Pro using video tracking software.
Professor emphasizes the importance of keeping the ball in the frame while filming.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: One dimensional motion. In this lab you will be measuring one dimensional motion of two objects,
yourself and a tennis ball. In the first part of the lab you will be walking back and forth
in front of a sonic motion detector. This makes chirps of sound which bounce off an object
and come back to the receiver to let longer pro calculate how far away that object must be.
You are going to be walking along some predetermined graphs that already exist in long pro
and you are going to be trying to match those graphs with the way your body moves.
There is a possibility that while you are doing this you are going to get aliasing effects which look like this.
These effects are due to the fact that if the sensor loses an echo it will assume the next echo is the missing one
and you will get drastically different positions because of that dropped echo.
This is most likely either due to this being aimed poorly or the fact that you as a person are not really a great echo material.
So think about what you could do to make yourself be a better echo material.
In the second part of the lab you are going to be throwing a tennis ball in front of your backdrop
as straight up and down as possible while filming it on one of our cameras.
After you film the ball track up and down you are going to import that video into longer pro
and analyze that motion using the longer pro's video tracking software.
By telling exactly where the ball is at any given frame of the video you can analyze this motion much as you did when you were walking in front of the sensor.
One thing that you need to know about these cameras is that since they can film in several different video modes
the viewfinder on the back of the camera is much bigger than the actual footage that will be recorded.
So make sure that you are lying up to the letterbox in the viewfinder when you are filming so that your motion doesn't go out of the frame of the video.
Thank you for staying to the end of the video. Here is this lab's fun fact.
The Stegosaurus had been extinct for at least 50 million years before Saturn's rings started to form.
